key: How know I that it is so with all the beauties of existing things? By this (nature of the Tao).
s: The chapter asks how it is known that it is so with all the beauties of existing things, and answers, by this; Wang Bi, on chapter 21, reads the question as how it is known that all things begin in non-being, and takes ‘this’ as what has been said above.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 21, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

evidence.words: 眾甫，物之始也。以無名說萬物始也。…此上之所云也。言吾何以知萬物之始於無哉，以此知之也。
evidence.gloss: ‘The many fathers’ are the beginning of things: the text explains the beginning of all things by the nameless. … ‘This’ is what has been said above. It means: how do I know that all things begin in non-being? I know it by this.
evidence.licence: public domain text; transcription CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource)

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 21, at [20]). Wang Bi’s base text reads 吾何以知眾甫之狀哉？以此 (Legge’s ‘all the beauties of existing things’ renders 眾甫 differently, but it is the same line); his comment on that line says ‘this’ is what was said above and glosses the question as how it is known that all things begin in non-being, exactly as the sentence has it. Plain sense restates the key verse and does not lean on Legge’s parenthesis. entry-check ok.
